text: Lesson 29 left both of Meridian's security groups wide open, with no inbound rules at all. This lesson closes that gap and adds the monitoring and cost guardrails an environment needs to count as operated, not just deployed — scoping access, replacing a hardcoded key with an IAM role, watching CPU, and guarding both the data and the bill.

meridian-web-sg gets exactly three inbound rules: HTTPS and HTTP open to the public internet, and SSH scoped to 203.0.113.0/24, Meridian's own office network, not to 0.0.0.0/0. meridian-app-sg gets one rule, scoped with --source-group sg-0meridianweb instead of an IP range, so only traffic actually coming from the web tier can reach port 8080.

meridian-app1 needs to read and write the S3 bucket from Lesson 29, and a key baked into its config file is a key that leaks the day that config ends up somewhere it shouldn't. An IAM role, an instance profile, and one associate-iam-instance-profile call give the instance temporary, auto-rotating credentials from its own metadata instead — nothing stored, nothing to rotate by hand.

A CloudWatch alarm on meridian-web1 watches CPUUtilization and fires only after two consecutive five-minute periods above 80 percent, publishing to an SNS topic so a real problem gets caught by a page instead of a customer complaint. A snapshot of the app tier's EBS volume protects the data itself the same way.

An AWS Budget guards something different — the bill. A $150 monthly budget with an 80-percent alert means Meridian's ops team hears about a cost problem from AWS directly, days before an invoice would ever show it, which is exactly the guardrail that opens Lesson 31's incident.

Scoped security groups, a role instead of a key, an alarm on CPU, a snapshot, and a budget — five guardrails layered onto the environment Lesson 29 built. Lesson 31 puts one of those guardrails to work, diagnosing a real connectivity problem on a newly launched instance from scratch.
